claims.text: Adding MoS2 to a refractory HEA matrix by spark plasma sintering will produce a composite combining high mechanical strength with stable, low-friction self-lubrication over a wide temperature range.
Refractory HEAs can possess high mechanical strength.
Refractory HEAs can retain useful properties at high temperatures.
NbMoTaW and CoCrFeNiTi are examples of refractory HEA matrices suitable for this application.
A refractory HEA can be consolidated from powder using spark plasma sintering.
MoS2 is a layered solid-lubricant phase.
The proposed composite can operate from room temperature to approximately 800–900 °C under severe mechanical stress.
Spark plasma sintering the HEA with MoS2 will create coherent interfaces and well-dispersed MoS2 lamellae.
Coherent HEA–MoS2 interfaces and dispersed MoS2 lamellae will facilitate sliding while preserving structural integrity.
The HEA matrix provides exceptional mechanical strength and thermal stability.
The intrinsic lamellar structure of MoS2 enables low-friction sliding in the proposed composite.
Spark plasma sintering promotes strong, coherent bonding at HEA–MoS2 interfaces.
Strong HEA–MoS2 interface bonding mitigates phase separation or degradation under thermal stress.
Adding MoS2 will significantly reduce friction coefficients relative to an HEA-only baseline.
Adding MoS2 will significantly reduce wear rates relative to an HEA-only baseline.
The MoS2-containing composite will maintain mechanical strength similar to that of the HEA-only baseline across the stated temperature range.
An HEA without a solid-lubricant phase has poorer tribological performance than the proposed composite.
The strength–lubrication balance depends on the volume fraction and dispersion quality of MoS2.
Extreme oxidative environments may reduce the stability of the MoS2 lubricant phase.
The optimal MoS2 content and SPS parameters for long-term cyclic thermal loading have not yet been determined.
